title: Geneva Conventions of 1949
summary: On 12 August 1949 a Swiss-convened conference in Geneva completed four treaties protecting wounded and sick soldiers, shipwrecked sailors, prisoners of war and, in a new treaty, civilians in enemy hands, with minimum rules for non-international conflicts in Common Article 3.
card: Delegates from 63 governments, meeting in Geneva from 21 April to 12 August 1949, rewrote the 1929 rules for the wounded and prisoners of war and added a fourth convention for civilians, drawing on the experience of the Second World War. A shared Article 3 set minimum standards for conflicts inside a state for the first time. The treaties took effect on 21 October 1950 and are now ratified by every state, though historians note that colonised peoples were poorly served by the drafting.
what:
On 12 August 1949 the Diplomatic Conference for the Establishment of International Conventions for the Protection of Victims of War closed in Geneva after four months of debate, having agreed four treaties. The First Convention covers wounded and sick members of armed forces on land, the Second the wounded, sick and shipwrecked at sea, the Third prisoners of war, and the Fourth civilian persons in time of war. The Swiss Federal Council convened the meeting, which sat from 21 April to 12 August 1949 under the Swiss Federal Councillor Max Petitpierre and was attended by 63 governments, 59 of which sent plenipotentiaries.

The texts revised earlier law that began with the 1864 Geneva Convention and was reworked in 1906 and 1929, together with the 1907 Hague convention applying the same principles to naval war. The Fourth Convention was new: the Second World War had shown that enemy civilians, internees and populations under occupation had little treaty protection. All four treaties open with a block of common provisions. Common Article 1 obliges states to respect the Conventions and to ensure respect for them in all circumstances. Common Article 2 applies them to declared wars, other armed conflicts between parties and occupation, even if one belligerent is not a party. Common Article 3 sets minimum standards of humane treatment, and forbids murder, torture, hostage-taking and sentencing without a proper court, in armed conflict not of an international character. Each treaty also requires states to punish grave breaches.

Seventeen delegations signed the four Conventions on 12 August 1949, forty-four further states signed before the signature period closed on 12 February 1950, and the Conventions entered into force on 21 October 1950. In 1977 two Additional Protocols extended protection, and a third followed in 2005. The Conventions are now universally ratified, with the UK National Archives giving 196 states. Scholars disagree on how to read the outcome: the ICRC and Swiss accounts present it as a humanitarian breakthrough, while analysts from the Global South stress that it left colonial wars largely outside its protection.

uncertainty.note: The date of adoption and signature of the Final Act is 12 August 1949 in the ICRC publication of the texts, the UK National Archives and the ICRC Library. The Conference itself ran 21 April to 12 August 1949. Signature continued: 17 delegations signed the Conventions on 12 August 1949, a second ceremony was held on 8 December 1949, the Soviet delegation signed four days later, and signature closed on 12 February 1950. Entry into force was 21 October 1950.

how: The path to the Conventions began in 1945, when the ICRC took up the task of revising the 1929 Convention on the wounded and sick, the Hague naval convention of 1907 and the 1929 prisoner-of-war Convention and drafting a civilians' convention. It held a meeting of experts in October 1945, a Preliminary Conference of National Red Cross Societies in July and August 1946, and in April 1947 a conference of government experts in which 70 representatives of 15 governments that had held many prisoners and internees agreed new texts. The drafts were adopted with amendments by the XVIIth International Red Cross Conference in Stockholm on 20 to 31 August 1948, attended by 50 governments and 52 national societies, and became the working papers of the Geneva conference. There four committees worked in parallel: one on the First and Second Conventions, one on prisoners of war, one on civilians, and a joint committee on common provisions. Their texts were harmonised by coordination and drafting committees, the Final Act was signed on 12 August 1949, and the Conventions came into force six months after two ratifications had been deposited. Switzerland acts as their depositary. Italy's use of chemical weapons in Ethiopia in 1935-1936, often linked to Mussolini's regime, falls under the separate 1925 Geneva Gas Protocol, signed on 17 June 1925 by 26 states, rather than under these four treaties.
why_it_matters:
The 1949 Conventions turned the experience of the Second World War into binding law that still governs how armies treat the people they capture, wound or occupy. Their most direct consequence was the Fourth Convention. Before it, civilians in enemy hands had no dedicated treaty; afterwards, protected persons were guaranteed humane treatment, collective punishment, reprisals against them and hostage-taking were prohibited, and unlawful deportation and torture were made grave breaches that states must prosecute. Common Article 3 carried minimum rules into civil wars, a field the earlier treaties had not touched, and later became the basis for the 1977 Additional Protocol II. Universal ratification means the rules bind every state, and the ICRC reports 174, 169 and 79 states party to the three Protocols.

A counterfactual shows what changed. In 1941-1945 Germany excused the starvation and killing of Soviet prisoners, 3.3 million of whom died, partly by pointing out that the USSR was not a party to the 1929 Convention. Under Common Article 2 of 1949, a state bound by the treaty must apply it toward a belligerent that is not a party, so that excuse is no longer available on those terms. Without the revision, wars after 1949 would have been fought under the 1929 prisoner-of-war text and Hague rules that focused chiefly on property in occupied lands.

The settlement was also incomplete. The Fourth Convention does not regulate the conduct of hostilities, and anti-colonial states complained that their wars were left outside the Conventions, which led to the 1977 Protocols and a continuing dispute with states such as the United States that have not accepted Protocol I.

related.because: The treatment of prisoners, enemy civilians and occupied populations in the Second World War exposed gaps in the 1929 Conventions and the absence of a civilians' treaty, and the Conventions were drafted explicitly to close them.

related.title: First Geneva Convention of 22 August 1864
related.because: The 1949 First Convention is the fourth revision of the 1864 treaty on the wounded, after the revisions of 1906 and 1929, so the 1949 system continues the line of law the 1864 text began.

related.title: Additional Protocols I and II to the Geneva Conventions (8 June 1977)
related.because: Gaps left by the 1949 texts, notably the lack of rules on the conduct of hostilities and on wars of self-determination, drove states and the ICRC to negotiate Additional Protocols I and II to supplement them. Protocol II in particular supplements Common Article 3.

perspectives.account: Present the Conventions as a decisive advance. States agreed in four months to revise the earlier treaties and add a civilians' convention, and the adoption of Common Article 3 is described as a breakthrough because earlier treaties covered only wars between states. They are said to be among the most universally accepted instruments of international law.

perspectives.holder: Srinivas Burra (South Asian University), writing from a Third World Approaches to International Law perspective
perspectives.account: The Conventions are both a break and a continuity. The Fourth Convention left the law of occupation largely as in the 1907 Hague Regulations, colonial peoples' experience of colonial wars got little attention although African, Asian and Latin American states were nearly half the participants, and Western states resisted naming colonial conflicts in Common Article 3, so those conflicts were treated as internal matters.

perspectives.holder: Delegates of some newly independent states at Geneva, such as Burma, as reported in EJIL: Talk!
perspectives.account: Not all Asian and African delegations wanted Common Article 3. The Burmese delegate, speaking for what he called Eastern countries, warned that applying the Conventions to internal conflicts could help those seeking power by undemocratic means, and noted that Great Powers had been reluctant to accept limits touching their own security; the provision was adopted in narrowed form. India, by contrast, supported a neutral emblem and later read Article 3 as covering anti-colonial conflict.

perspectives.holder: Anti-colonial delegations at the 1974-1977 conference and the United States (Reagan administration)
perspectives.account: Newly independent states argued that the 1949 texts left colonial and racist-regime wars outside the law of international conflict and secured Article 1(4) in Protocol I; the United States objected that this imported a 'just war' concept, and in 1987 President Reagan declined to send Protocol I to the Senate, saying the United States would not give protection to terrorist groups as the price for progress in humanitarian law.
